title: Keeossechok, Sachem of the Secatogue
summary: Keeossechok was a Secatogue sachem whose clearest surviving record is the June 1, 1657 Five Necks deed for South Shore meadow lands.
content:
Keeossechok was a Secatogue sachem whose clearest surviving record is the June 1, 1657 Five Necks deed for South Shore meadow lands. That deed documents his leadership, but the cited sources do not establish his birth or death dates.

The surviving evidence for Keeossechok is brief, so the history stays close to the deed and place-name sources rather than filling in undocumented family or life details.2

Historical Context

The Five Necks deed names Keeossechok as Sachem of the Secatogue and records him alongside Wyandanch in a sale of meadow necks on the south side of Long Island.3

His connected places are broad approximations around Secatogue Neck, West Islip/Babylon, Bay Shore, and the Great South Bay marshlands. The sources support a regional connection, not an exact private or sensitive point.13

References

  1. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent, p. 234.
  2. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700, Appendix C, p. 299.
  3. Brewster-Walker research materials preserving the June 1, 1657 Five Necks deed transcription, pp. 49-50.
why_this_matters: Keeossechok matters because even sparse deed records preserve named Secatogue leadership and show that South Shore marshes, necks, and bays were Native homelands before colonial town boundaries remade the map.
